statement: The system shall help users spot problems early.
The system shall help users quickly understand which part of the system is likely causing a problem.
The system shall support action before equipment performance degrades.
The system shall support action before a failure becomes obvious.
The system shall initially detect high-value faults in chillers and cooling towers.
The system shall detect sensor issues.
The system shall detect abnormal temperatures or pressures.
The system shall detect poor heat transfer.
The system shall detect valve problems.
The system shall detect pump problems.
The system shall detect fan faults.
The system shall detect motor faults.
The system shall detect general efficiency losses.
The system shall provide a clear likely fault as a recommendation.
The system shall provide the evidence behind the likely fault.
The system shall provide a practical next step.
The system shall support checking a sensor as a practical next step.
The system shall support inspecting a component as a practical next step.
The system shall support verifying setpoints as a practical next step.
The system shall support scheduling maintenance as a practical next step.
Operators shall use the system for routine monitoring.
Operators shall use the system for alarm triage.
Technicians shall use the system results to guide troubleshooting during site visits.
Technicians shall use the system results to guide remote diagnostics.
The diagnostic tool shall use a layered approach to separate likely sensor problems from real equipment faults before assigning blame to a component.
When several faults fit the same symptoms, the diagnostic tool shall rank the faults by likelihood and impact.
When the result is ambiguous, the diagnostic tool shall clearly indicate the ambiguity rather than forcing a single answer.
The diagnostic tool shall treat repeated sensor anomalies as a stronger signal only if they persist over time and align with other operating data.
If repeated sensor anomalies do not persist over time or do not align with other operating data, the diagnostic tool shall flag them as possibly intermittent instrumentation issues.
The diagnostic tool shall use a confidence threshold below which it raises a warning or needs-review state.
The diagnostic tool shall make a more specific diagnostic recommendation when confidence is above the threshold.
The diagnostic tool shall use the core operating sensor points for the chiller and cooling-tower subsystems.
The diagnostic tool shall use temperature readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use pressure readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use flow readings where available.
The diagnostic tool shall use valve position readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use fan status readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use motor status readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use power or current readings if the site has them.
The diagnostic tool shall use equipment specifications.
The diagnostic tool shall use the control sequence or configuration.
The diagnostic tool shall use setpoints.
The diagnostic tool shall use the asset operating mode.
The diagnostic tool shall consider whether the unit is starting, running normally, or being staged off when interpreting readings.
The diagnostic tool shall use ambient conditions and weather information if available.
The diagnostic tool shall use ambient conditions and weather information for cooling-tower performance analysis.
The diagnostic tool shall use basic asset metadata including make, model, and capacity.
The diagnostic tool shall use information about whether any components have been overridden or taken out of service.
The diagnostic logic shall recognize the main operating states that change the meaning of readings, including startup, normal run, standby, staging, shutdown, and maintenance or test mode.
In the recognized operating states, the same symptom shall be treated as expected or as a fault only if it persists beyond the normal transition period.
If a component is bypassed, manually overridden, or marked out of service, the tool shall reduce how strongly it ranks faults on that component.
The tool shall note bypassed, manually overridden, or out-of-service conditions clearly.
The diagnostic tool shall compare current behavior against both short-term history and a learned normal baseline.
The learned baseline shall be updated carefully so that bad behavior is not learned as normal.
The diagnostic tool shall require a sustained deviation before declaring a fault.
When performance is drifting but not yet clearly broken, the diagnostic tool shall flag it as an early warning and rank it below a confirmed fault.
The system shall provide different explanation content based on the user's role.
For operators, the system shall present a short practical summary that includes the suspected fault, confidence, and immediate action.

For technicians, the system shall present the supporting evidence, key sensor trends, the rule or pattern that triggered the diagnosis, and related conditions that help verify the diagnosis in the field.
For facilities managers, the system shall present an intermediate-level explanation focused on equipment condition, risk, and whether the issue requires scheduling or escalation.
The system shall show traceability back to the data it used to produce the diagnosis.
Access to diagnostic results, explanations, and related functions shall vary by user role.
Operators shall be able to view live diagnostics.
Operators shall be able to acknowledge issues or comment on issues.
Facilities managers shall have broader view access.
Technicians shall be able to see deeper diagnostics.
Control functions such as changing thresholds or diagnostic settings shall be limited to authorized admin users.
Remote service staff shall have access only to assets assigned to them.
The system shall integrate with the BMS or SCADA system to obtain live operating data and basic equipment status.
The system shall integrate with a historian, if one exists, to obtain trends and older data.
The system shall connect to the CMMS or work-order system so that confirmed issues or high-priority diagnoses can be turned into maintenance requests.
The system shall push only meaningful notifications for alarms.
The system shall sync equipment record asset IDs, points, and configuration details so diagnostics remain aligned with the installed equipment.
The system shall route notifications to the appropriate people based on severity and asset ownership.
The system shall send immediate alerts to operators for urgent conditions.
The system shall escalate unresolved issues to facilities managers.
The system shall re-open or re-alert when a condition clears and then recurs.
The system shall re-evaluate active faults and important status changes in near real time.
The system shall perform slower scheduled reviews for lower-priority trend checks.
The system shall automatically escalate an issue that remains unresolved for a set period.
The system shall refresh the baseline when the equipment has a real change in configuration.
The system shall revisit the baseline periodically.
The system shall wait for enough clean data before retraining the baseline.
The system shall exclude periods with known faults from baseline learning.
The system shall exclude periods with overrides from baseline learning.
The system shall exclude commissioning periods from baseline learning.
The system shall exclude shutdown transients from baseline learning.
The system shall exclude sensor failures from baseline learning.

The system should rely on event markers where possible to identify periods excluded from training data.
The system should use maintenance logs as event markers.
The system should use occupancy or schedule changes as event markers.
The system should use manual overrides as event markers.
The system should use known equipment state changes from the BMS or CMMS as event markers.
Where explicit markers are unavailable, the system should use simple site rules to exclude unwanted data.
The system should exclude startup and shutdown windows from training data.
The system should exclude periods with unstable sensor readings from training data.
The system should exclude data right after a reset or repair from training data.
The system should apply a short stabilization period after commissioning or maintenance before considering data clean enough to learn from.
The stabilization period after commissioning or maintenance should be site-specific.
The system should either tag abnormal weather periods separately or exclude them from the baseline unless a weather-adjusted model is explicitly desired.
The system shall diagnose HVAC faults from operating data and equipment information.
The system shall support operators, facilities staff, and technicians in using the diagnostic results for day-to-day maintenance and remote monitoring.

The system shall exclude routine automated system activity from the audit trail unless it changes something material.
The system shall not expose full before-and-after values broadly in sensitive cases.
Whether before-and-after values are hidden, limited, or shown should depend on the sensitivity of the data.
Whether before-and-after values are hidden, limited, or shown should depend on the customer’s site policy.
Whether before-and-after values are hidden, limited, or shown should depend on the role of the person reviewing it.
Detailed operating history and customer-specific configuration changes may need tighter restrictions than a simple label correction or a generic status update.
If there is any doubt, access to before-and-after values should be limited to authorized administrators.
For investigations, maintenance events, or comparing results over time, the diagnostic should use a snapshot taken at a specific timestamp.
When the plant is in a steady operating state and the data is complete and recent, the system can present the result with higher confidence and normal context.

In cases where confidence is lower, the system should provide extra context such as recent trend movement or the reason for the uncertainty so the operator understands why the diagnosis is less certain.

The system shall provide operators with information they can act on during continuity disruptions.

Maintenance records shall take precedence for configuration or service status information.
Live sensor values shall take precedence for current operating conditions information.
If no authoritative source has been set, the system shall flag the conflict, use the most recent trusted data available, and indicate that the result may require human review.
If multiple plausible terms exist, the system shall show the preferred site term as the main label and keep the other terms as aliases or notes.
The system shall make the result immediately understandable.
Operators or technicians should be allowed to view or export raw data when they are troubleshooting, commissioning, or validating why a diagnosis was produced.
Access to raw data for troubleshooting, commissioning, or diagnosis validation should be more restricted than the normal results view.
Raw points or configuration details should be hidden unless the user has the right role.
The exact approval steps should remain undecided for now.
Only trained technicians, service engineers, and authorized administrators should be able to view or change underlying configuration.
The system shall retain the audit trail long enough to support troubleshooting in normal operation.
The system shall not discard the audit trail sooner just because a contract ends if there is still a business need or a retention requirement.
The default diagnosis explanation shall state what to check next.
The default diagnosis explanation shall not overwhelm the user with every intermediate calculation.
Near-real-time monitoring diagnostics should be considered stale if they are more than a few minutes old.
A slower update rate is acceptable for trending.
A slower update rate is acceptable for energy review.
A slower update rate is acceptable for noncritical faults.
Faster reaction is required for alarms.
Faster reaction is required for equipment protection.

The system shall switch to urgent fault detection when the asset is critical enough that a missed fault could cause immediate downtime.
